text:
Chicago Italian beef discourse has gotten weird.
Ever since The Bear, we’ve turned a working-class sandwich into a hype contest.

But the Italian beef was never about clout.
It was born from Italian immigrants stretching tough cuts of meat, slow-roasting them, slicing them thin, dunking them in gravy, and feeding whole communities. Standing up. Dripping everywhere. No frills.

That’s why neighborhood spots still matter.

Johnny’s Beef & Gyros is exactly that.
A family-run Chicago staple doing it right.

Order it dipped, with hot giardiniera and mozzarella.
Razor-thin beef soaked in rich au jus. Soft, gravy-logged bread that still holds together. Crunchy, spicy giardiniera cutting through the fat. Gooey mozzarella melting everything into one chaotic, perfect bite.

Don’t skip the Greek fries.
Fried in beef tallow, tossed with olive oil, oregano, feta, and lemon. Crispy, savory, salty, and bright. A Mediterranean twist that somehow still feels deeply Chicago.

And yes, get the pizza puff. Always.

You don’t need to sit in traffic for 45 minutes to eat a great Italian beef.
Sometimes the best one is a few blocks away, made by people who actually feed the neighborhood.

Support the spots that built this city.
Stop confusing hype with heritage.

Save this for your next beef run.
Share it with someone who thinks only the “big names” matter.

More important, he had the courage to have empathy towards all.

text:
The Slow Cooker Meal Prep Series has hit over 125 MILLION views across platforms 🤯

The bulk approach to meal prepping has been a game changer for me (there's no better feeling than having a freezer stocked with 60-70+ high protein meals, ready to go whenever) - so it's awesome to see so many of y'all feel the same 🙏

The slow cooker is the ultimate tool for making bulk meal prep as simple as possible

My content has been focused on meal prep for quite a while now - and there's a few things l've learned since making meal prepping my full time job 👇

1.) Freezing meal preps is essential. From a pure taste perspective - meal preps stored frozen retain flavor and freshness FAR BETTER than anything stored in the fridge. I've found that food stored for a month frozen tastes better than food stored in the fridge for just 24 hours. Equally as important - if you store meal preps frozen, there isn't "pressure" to finish them within 5-7 days to avoid them going bad. Aka - your meal preps aren't a ticking time bomb. Freezing meal preps allows you to build a massive stockpile of meals in your freezer that are available whenever you want them

2.) This ties into the first point - but meal prep in BULK. Find a recipe you like, and scale it to make 10+ servings (I know some people take my recipes and scale them up to 20 serving meals). Again, freezing is essential here so that you can store meals for the long term + don't have to eat the same thing 10 straight days

3.) Lastly, and by far the most important if you want to succeed with meal prep: the meals have to taste amazing and be something you genuinely look forward to eating. You want your meal preps to sound better than anything you could get at the food court. I have tons of free recipes on my feed for you to try out, and an entire meal prep cookbook with 100+ high protein recipes built to make the process as enjoyable as possible (and yes, an entirely slow cooker focused cookbook is coming later this year)

Let me know what recipes you want to see next as part of this series!

💥 Sheet Pan Kebabs (So Easy & Delicious)

Kebab Ingredients:
2 lb ground beef
1 small white onion, grated
3 garlic cloves, minced
¼ cup fresh dill, chopped
¼ cup fresh parsley, chopped
Zest of ½ lemon
Pinch of black pepper
Pinch of salt
1 tbsp cumin
1 tbsp smoked paprika
1 tsp coriander
¼ tsp cinnamon

Yogurt Sauce:
¾ cup Greek Yogurt
Juice of ½ lemon
1.5 tbsp Olive oil
1 tsp Date syrup
Pinch of salt
Pinch of black pepper
Parsley, freshly chopped
Dill, freshly chopped

Directions:
1. Preheat the oven to 425F.
2. Add all kebab ingredients to a large bowl and mix with your hands. Once thoroughly
mixed in, spray a sheet pan with avocado or olive oil, then toss the meat onto it and
press the meat evenly across making a rough rectangle. It should be about ½-¾ inch
thick.
3. Score long vertical lines almost to the bottom (don’t cut through), both vertically and
horizontally creating your kebabs. Bake for 20–22 mins.
4. While they bake in the oven, combine all your yogurt sauce ingredients in a bowl until it
becomes a creamy consistency.
5. Remove the kebabs from the oven. Spoon out excess liquid, mix with 1 tbsp tomato paste, and brush over kebabs. Broil for 2-3 mins until browned.
6. Let rest a few minutes, then cut along the score lines
7. Enjoy as delicious wrap with the yogurt sauce, tomatoes, and lettuce, or eat as is with the sauce.

text:
Homemade Chick-fil-a :)

Chick-fil-a sauce

½ cup mayonnaise 
3 Tbsp barbecue sauce
2 Tbsp honey
2 Tbsp yellow mustard
½ Tsp kosher salt 
½ black pepper
½ a lemon juiced

Chicken Brine

4 boneless skinless chicken thighs 
1 cups buttermilk
1 cup pickle juice
1 Tbsp paprika
1 ½ Tbsp garlic powder
1 tsp cayenne
1 tsp white pepper
1 tsp onion powder
1 Tbsp kosher salt

Dry Drede 

2 cups all purpose flour
½ cup potato starch
1 Tbsp paprika
1 Tbsp garlic powder
1 tsp onion powder
1 tsp MSG (optional)
1 Tbsp kosher salt
2 ½ tsp cayenne 
1 tsp ground black pepper

Waffle Fries

3 large russet potatoes
1 ½ Tbsp white vinegar
1 Tbsp salt
1.5 qt vegetable oil for frying

Pickles

1 small english cucumber or ½ a large one, sliced into thin rounds 
1 Tbsp pickling spice
1 cup white vinegar
1 cup water
2 Tbsp sugar
1 tsp MSG optional 
2 Tbsp kosher salt
2 sprigs dill

Assembly 

4 burger buns
4 slices pepper jack 
1 small head butter lettuce,
1 beefsteak tomato, thinly sliced
Lemonade (for the traditional experience) 

For the Chick-fil-a sauce, in a mixing bowl add, mayonnaise, barbecue sauce, honey, yellow mustard, kosher salt, black pepper and lemon. Mix until fully combined and set aside in the fridge. 

For the pickles, add your sliced cucumber to your mason jar along with the dill and pickling spice. In your sauce pot add white vinegar, water, sugar, MSG and kosher salt. Bring to a simmer then pour into the mason jar. Screw the lid on, let cool then refrigerate while you prep everything else. 

Prep the fries. Peel your potatoes and cut on a slice once on a wavy  mandoline, quarter turn, slice again and so on and so forth to get your waffle fries. If you don't have a wavy mandoline, you can cut the potatoes normally.

Add the potatoes to a large bowl and cover with ice water. Mix well to remove the starch, drain and set aside. 

Fill a large pot ⅔ the way with water, cover with a lid and bring to a boil. Once boiling add, white vinegar and salt.
 
Add your fries carefully to the pot and cook for about 2-3 minutes until slightly soft but not fully cooked. When you break one in half it should not snap like it's raw but it should be cooked with slight resistance. Make sure not to over cook this. Remove your potatoes to a couple of wire racks to cool. 

Heat your frying oil in a large pot to 330°F.

Carefully add your fries in batches and fry for 1-2 minutes until par cooked but not golden. Remove to a wire rack and set aside while we work on our chicken.

Chicken Brine: To a large bowl add, buttermilk, pickle juice, kosher salt, black pepper, garlic powder, onion powder, paprika, cayenne and MSG. Add your chicken, mix well to coat and set aside in the fridge for 1 hour to overnight. Or use right away. 

In a large bowl add all purpose flour, potato starch, kosher salt, black pepper, garlic powder, onion powder, paprika, cayenne and whisk to combine. Remove the chicken from the fridge. Coat the chicken in the dry dredge with no bald spots then dip back in the wet brine then back in the dry with no bald spots. Place your coated chicken on a wire rack and set aside.

Heat your oil to 350° F. Once your oil is up to temp, fry your chicken, 2 pieces at a time for about 6-8 minutes, until fully cooked and golden brown and crispy. Remove to a wire rack and repeat with all your chicken. 

Heat your oil to 375°F. 

Carefully add your par cooked fries to the oil in batches and fry for 1-2 minutes until beautiful golden brown and crispy. Remove to a wire rack and season generously with salt. 

Assembly, on a toasted bun add sauce, pickles, lettuce, tomato, chicken and cheese. melt however possible then add the sauced top bun. Serve with the fries and lemonade. Enjoy!

When performing rows, whether the focus is geared more towards lats or upper back — the same rules apply here.

Don’t drop your sternum or chest down. Stay neutral. 

Don’t let your wrists collapse in. Always keep your wrist in line with the elbow. This oftens happens as a result of people trying to pull through their hand, rather than the upper arm / elbow.

Don’t arch your back. The only thing this does is allow you to overcompensate & take tension away from the target muscle. 

If you’re using a chest supported row, then you should be pushing yourself forward into the pad to produce counterforce — as you pull the weight back.

If i just started golf. Part 1

Thinking back, i think if i fixed my swing in this order, i would have saved myself alot of time. 

1. Grip - changing the grip later is such a pain, so just start with a neutral grip and if needed you can adjust slightly as you get better. Yes you can play good golf with a strong or weak grip, but better to start as neutral. 

2. Setup - im sure youve seen it too. The guy on the first tee with the odd setup. You know the swing is going to be just as odd, and it almost has to be. 

I think setup is important because It means less adjustments you have to do in the swing to get to a good impact position. 

3. Swaying - so hard to have a good consistent swing with ‘alot’ of swaying on the backswing. It just puts you in a position to do a whole lot of bad things. 

4. Early extension - think ive talked about this enough

text:
Split Stance Dumbbell Curls - now first off, how I do curls (with elbow coming up, which does inclue a bit of front delt action) might be different than how you've learned it. That's NOT the key point of this video!

I find this raise of the elbow is good for getting a bit more bicep activation at the top, due to where the bicep originates in the shoulder. You can do them however you like!

The key point here is the split stance for dumbbell (or barbell) curls.

When you do any sort of curl with your feet in line horizontally, you create a thinner base of support.

When the weight comes up to the midpoint, this puts the load out in front of your base of support, which means your body has to compensate by leaning back.  When then creates more incentive to cheat and heave.

This is actually more of an issue on barbell curls but it does happen with dumbbell curls as well.

Essentially, all you need to do to fix this is set your feet in a split stance.

This creates a larger base of support so that you can keep your upper body still while you do whatever curl variation you're doing.

It's a simple setup tweak that can have an immediately impact.

text:
Poutine! 🇨🇦

Fries

3 large russet potatoes, washed and cut into ⅓ inch strips
1 Tbsp white vinegar
2 tsp salt
2 tsp baking soda
3 qt frying oil
Kosher salt

Gravy 

3 ½  cups good beef stock (homemade preferably) 
1 small bunch fresh thyme
3 sprigs fresh rosemary 
¼ cup dried shiitake mushrooms
4 Tbsp unsalted butter
3 cloves garlic, minced
1 large shallot, finely diced
3 Tbsp all purpose flour
1 Tbsp worcestershire sauce
1 Tbsp dark soy sauce

Assembly

16 oz cheese curds
Parsley leaves

Fries, to start, fill a large bowl with cold water. 

Wash and cut your potatoes into ⅓ inch strips and add them to the water. Mix well to remove some of the starch then drain off the water. 

Fill a large pot ⅔ of the way with water and bring to a boil. Once boiling add, white vinegar, baking soda and salt. 

Blanching: Add your fries carefully to the pot and cook for about 2 minutes until slightly soft but not fully cooked. When you break one in half it should not snap like it's raw but it should be cooked with slight resistance. Make sure not to over cook this. Remove your fries to a couple of wire racks to cool. 

First fry: Heat your frying oil in a large pot to 330°F.

Carefully add your fries in batches and fry for 1-2 minutes until par cooked but not golden. Remove to a wire rack and set aside while we make our gravy.

Infused stock: Add your beef stock to a medium pot along with fresh thyme, rosemary and shiitakes. Set over medium, bring to a simmer then pour into a heat proof container to infuse for 15-20 minutes then remove the aromatics.

Gravy: Clean your pot then set over medium-low. Add the butter, once melted add the shallot and garlic. Season with salt and cook for 2-3 minutes until softened. Add the flour. Cook for 1-2 minutes and while whisking, gradually add your stock. Once thickened, finally add worcestershire sauce and soy sauce. Season to taste with salt & pepper. Keep warm. 

Heat your oil to 375°F. 

Second fry: Carefully add your par cooked fries to the oil in batches and fry for 1-2 minutes until beautiful golden brown and crispy. Remove to a wire rack and season generously with salt. 

Assembly:To assemble on a plate, fries, cheese curds, gravy then more fries, cheese curds and generous gravy. Garnish with parsley. Enjoy!
